characters.Sarah Quill: Baker, heroine, point of view in odd chapters, early thirties. Runs the bakery on Lantern Street. Came back to Larkmere when her great-aunt Fenna Quill died and left her the shop. Her bread carries whatever she feels while shaping it. She promised herself one season, then she would decide whether to stay. When she holds the point of view the voice is warm and sensory, quick to notice heat, hands, flour and rising dough, and her comparisons come from baking.
characters.Jack Mercer: Ferryman, hero, point of view in even chapters, mid thirties. Pilots the ferry Heron across Larkmere Water. Quiet, dry humor, steady hands. Believes the ferry is the only place he is allowed to be sure of himself. Notices what people carry and never says it first. When he holds the point of view the voice is dry, spare and watchful, and his comparisons come from water, lines, current and the tiller. Baking comparisons stay out of his chapters and water comparisons stay out of hers.
characters.Odalys Pike: Innkeeper, Sarah's friend, late thirties. Runs the Lamplight Inn, reads faces, teases Sarah without mercy. Wants her friend happy and cannot keep that to herself.
characters.Nell Mercer: Jack's niece, deckhand, sixteen. Works the lines on the ferry. Sharp, loyal, sees everything between her uncle and the baker long before either admits it. Only ever meddles, never anywhere near the intimate moments.
characters.Gideon Teague: Old townsman, lantern keeper, past seventy. Lights the harbor lanterns each dusk. Knew Fenna Quill for fifty years. Speaks little, and what he says tends to matter.
characters.Fenna Quill: Sarah's great-aunt, deceased before the story opens, died in her eighties. Baked in the shop for sixty years. Her recipes are written in a margin language of small marks that Sarah is slowly learning to read.

plot_facts: Sarah's bread carries the feeling she has while shaping it. Calm hands make calm bread. Longing makes bread that makes whoever eats it ache and look toward the water.

A kiss given in love sets a loaf's feeling for good. Sarah fears that if she kisses Jack, every loaf she bakes will say it aloud to the whole town, and she will have lost the choice of when and how to tell anyone.

Jack believes the ferry keeps its people. Fenna loved a ferryman once, and he left on the last run of a season. Jack will not ask Sarah to stay because he thinks wanting her to stay is the same as trapping her.
The Heron will not carry a lie across the water. It drifts slow and sulks when anyone aboard hides what they feel. The more they hide, the later the crossing.
Harbor lanterns are lit at dusk. Whoever stands at the same lantern when it catches is said to be thinking of the same person.

Larkmere is a small fictional lakeside town on Larkmere Water. Sarah's bakery is on Lantern Street. Jack pilots the ferry Heron across the lake. Odalys Pike runs the Lamplight Inn. Gideon Teague lights the harbor lanterns at dusk.
Odd chapters are told from Sarah's point of view and even chapters from Jack's, in close third person, past tense.
Writing rule: The love story is the book. Every chapter raises the ache by one notch, all the way to the last page.
Writing rule: Desire lives in small physical detail: the weight of a hand, the distance between two shoulders, breath on a collar, the pause before a sentence, the effort of staying still.

Writing rule: Pressed closeness (rungs 4 and up) is built from restraint. Show what the body does to hold back: a locked grip, a held breath, eyes fixed on a point, a word not said. Sensual, never explicit.
Writing rule: Never let the obstacle be a meeting, a ruling, a debt, a count or any procedure. Interruptions come from feeling, weather, magic, or a person who loves them.
Writing rule: No dates, weekdays, ages in digits or phrases like three days later. Time is season, light, weather and the bread.
Writing rule: Show the bread magic in every chapter, small and specific.
Writing rule: After the kiss the longing does not ease. Every chapter wants more than the one before, and the book releases it only in the final chapter. Never plot machinery.
Writing rule: Nell never appears in any intimate beat. She only meddles around the edges.
Writing rule: No em dashes. Avoid tidy summary sentences at chapter ends. Let the last image carry the feeling.
